meta.note: Period boundaries are conventions and vary by source.

periods.text: Archaic period ca. 700-480 BC (Pyrgos Museum: Orientalising 700-610, Archaic 610-490/480).
periods.label: evidence

periods.text: Classical period ca. 480-323 BC, including Persian Wars (490-479), Delian League, Peloponnesian War (431-404); ends with Alexander's death 323 BC.
periods.label: evidence

periods.text: Hellenistic period 323-31 BC; ends conventionally with the Battle of Actium (31 BC). Successor kingdoms: Seleucids, Ptolemies, Antigonids.
periods.label: evidence

periods.text: Roman rule over the Greek mainland 146 BC-330 AD.
periods.label: evidence

periods.text: Minoan civilisation flourished 2800-1100 BCE; Mycenaean civilisation spread 1600-1100 BC.
periods.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Delos: by legend the birthplace of Apollo and Artemis; called 'the most sacred of all islands' (Callimachus).
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Delphi: Pan-Hellenic sanctuary of Apollo and oracle of the Pythia; regarded as the omphalos (centre of the world).
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Mycenae: the kingdom of the mythical Agamemnon; Mycenaean culture inspired Homer's epics.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Olympia: centre of the worship of Zeus.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Hesiod, Theogony: Aphrodite grew from the sea-foam, drew near Cythera, then came to Cyprus - hence Cytherea and Cyprogenes.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Hesiod, Theogony: Rhea was sent to Lyctus in Crete to bear Zeus; Earth hid him in a cave on Mount Aegeum and Cronos was given a stone in swaddling clothes.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Hesiod, Theogony opens with the Heliconian Muses; Works and Days mentions Hesiod dedicating a tripod to the Muses of Helicon.
myths_places.label: evidence
myths_places.citation: Hesiod, Theogony ll. 1-25; Works and Days 651-9

myths_places.text: Homeric Hymn to Apollo: Leto sought a place to bear Apollo; he was born on Delos, which he claimed as his chosen seat.
myths_places.label: evidence
myths_places.citation: Homeric Hymn to Apollo ll. 1-178 (Delian part: Delos/Cynthus ll. 1-29, Leto and Delos ll. 30-101, birth ll. 115-139)

myths_places.text: Homeric Hymn to Apollo: Apollo founds his temple at Crisa below Parnassus (Pytho), slays the she-dragon, and in dolphin form brings Cretan priests.
myths_places.label: evidence
myths_places.citation: Homeric Hymn to Apollo ll. 254-286 (Crisa), ll. 334-374 (dragoness, naming of Pytho)

myths_places.text: Iliad, Catalogue of Ships: those who held 'the strong city of Mycenae, rich Corinth and Cleonae' sent a hundred ships.
myths_places.label: evidence (book) + inference (card adjacency)
myths_places.citation: Iliad 2, Catalogue of Ships - Perseus card 2.560-599 (follows Tiryns at end of card 2.520-559)

myths_places.text: Iliad: the Greeks were detained at Aulis on their way to Troy.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Iliad: Troy is the setting; the archaeological site of Troy has 4,000 years of history.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Odyssey: Odysseus's home is Ithaca; Telemachus voyages to Pylos and Sparta.
myths_places.label: evidence (book-level only)
myths_places.citation: Odyssey Book IX (Ithaca) per Butler; Telemachus to Pylos/Sparta Books III-IV (book-level)

myths_places.text: Odyssey: Odysseus reaches Scheria, land of the Phaeacians; Circe lives on the Aeaean island; the Sun's cattle are on the Thrinacian island; Calypso on Ogygia. (Real-world locations are uncertain/debated.)
myths_places.label: evidence
myths_places.citation: Odyssey: Ogygia Book I; Scheria Book V; Aeaea Book X; Thrinacia Book XI (Butler book headings)

myths_places.text: Pausanias 2.1.3-4: at Cromyon Theseus overcame the sow Phaea; at the Isthmus he killed the brigand Sinis, who tore victims apart with pine trees.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 2.1.6: Corinthians say Poseidon and Helius disputed the land; Briareos gave Poseidon the Isthmus and Helius the height (Acrocorinth), later handed to Aphrodite (2.4.6).
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 2.3.2: Peirene was a woman who became a spring through tears for her son Cenchrias, killed by Artemis.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 2.3.6-7: the Well of Glauce and the tomb of Medea's children at Corinth.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 2.7.7: after killing Pytho, Apollo and Artemis came to Aegialea (Sicyon) for purification.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 2.13.7: Phlius claimed an Omphalos, 'the center of all the Peloponnesus', and a House of Divination where Amphiaraus first divined.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 2.14.1: at Celeae mysteries of Demeter were held every fourth year, modelled on Eleusis.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Paphos includes Nea Paphos, 'Aphrodite's Sacred City'.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 10.5.5-6: earliest oracle at Delphi belonged to Earth (prophetess Daphnis); Earth gave her share to Themis, who gave it to Apollo; Poseidon received Calaureia in exchange.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 10.5.9-13: Delphic legends of five temples - laurel, beeswax and feathers, bronze, stone (Trophonius and Agamedes), and the present one by Spintharus of Corinth.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 10.6.5-6: the city was called Pytho because Apollo's victim rotted (pythesthai) there; poets call it a dragon set by Earth to guard the oracle.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 10.16.3: the Omphalus of white marble, said by Delphians to be the centre of all the earth.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 10.8.9: the spring of Castalia on the way up to the sanctuary.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 10.5.3-4: the Cleft Road (Schiste) where Oedipus killed his father Laius; tombs of Laius and his servant at the meeting of three roads.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 10.4.4: at Panopeus, clay-coloured stones said to be remains of the clay from which Prometheus fashioned mankind.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 10.12.1-5: the rock where the Sibyl Herophile chanted oracles at Delphi.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 5.7.6-9: Elean antiquaries say Idaean Heracles first held the Olympic games, crowning the winner with wild olive.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 5.7.2-3: Alpheius pursued Arethusa to Ortygia (Syracuse), where the river mingles with her spring.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 5.10.2-9: temple of Zeus at Olympia (architect Libon), image by Pheidias; east pediment shows the chariot race of Pelops and Oenomaus, west the Lapiths and Centaurs.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 5.13.1-6: the Pelopium, and the shoulder-blade of Pelops recovered from the sea.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 5.6.7-8: Mount Typaeum, from which women caught at the games were by law thrown; Callipateira's story.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 1.24.5: Parthenon pediments show the birth of Athena and the contest of Athena and Poseidon for the land.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 1.26.5 and 1.27.2: in the Erechtheum, sea-water and a trident mark (Poseidon's claim); the olive produced by Athena, said to have regrown after the Persian burning.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 1.22.4-5: from the bastion of Wingless Victory, Aegeus is said to have thrown himself down on seeing Theseus's black sails.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 1.28.5: Hill of Ares (Areopagus) - Ares the first tried there, later Orestes.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 1.18.2: the daughters of Cecrops opened Erichthonius's chest and threw themselves from the Acropolis.
myths_places.label: evidence

myths_places.text: Pausanias 1.27.10: Theseus drove the Marathonian bull to the Acropolis; Minos's tribute of seven maidens and seven boys for the Minotaur at Cnossus.
myths_places.label: evidence

sites.text: Acropolis of Athens; fortified since 13th c. BC; cult of Athena from 8th c. BC; UNESCO 1987.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Delphi, on Mt Parnassus slopes; oracle developed from 8th c. BC; UNESCO 1987.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Olympia, Elis, at confluence of Alpheios and Kladeos; UNESCO 1989.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Delos, Cyclades; free port after 167 BC; UNESCO 1990.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Sanctuary of Asklepios at Epidaurus.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Mycenae and Tiryns, Argolis; UNESCO 1999.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Minoan Palatial Centres (Knossos, Phaistos, Malia, Zakros, Zominthos, Kydonia), Crete; UNESCO 2025.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Troy (Türkiye): 4,000 years of history; first contact between Anatolia and the Mediterranean world.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Paestum and Velia within Cilento (Italy); Greek colonists among successive occupants.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Syracuse and Pantalica (Sicily): ancient Greek town and rock necropolis.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Agrigento, Valley of the Temples (Sicily): Greek colony founded 6th c. BCE.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Pompeii, Herculaneum, Torre Annunziata (Italy).
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Megalithic Temples of Malta, 4th-3rd millennium BC; among earliest free-standing stone buildings.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Carthage (Tunisia): founded by Phoenicians; Punic metropolis and later Roman provincial capital.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Leptis Magna (Libya): Phoenician port of 7th c. BCE, embellished by the Severans.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Cyrene (Libya).
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Byblos (Lebanon): continuously inhabited since Neolithic; witness to the beginnings of Phoenician civilisation.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Paphos (Cyprus): Nea Paphos and Kouklia.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Butrint (Albania), ~20 km from Saranda.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Ephesus (Türkiye): settlement from 7th millennium BCE; shifting shoreline relocated the city.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Pergamon (Türkiye): Attalid capital founded 3rd c. BC.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Hierapolis-Pamukkale (Türkiye): Hellenistic spa town above travertine terraces.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Xanthos-Letoon (Türkiye): Lycian civilisation.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Medieval City of Rhodes (Knights of St John 1309-1523).
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Aigai/Vergina: royal capital of Macedon, Temenid dynasty of Philip II and Alexander.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Temple of Apollo Epicurius at Bassae, Arcadia, 2nd half 5th c. BC.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Pythagoreion and Heraion of Samos.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Philippi: refounded by Philip II 356 BCE on the Via Egnatia; later Roman colony.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Memphis and its Necropolis - Pyramid Fields from Giza to Dahshur (Egypt).
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Ancient Thebes (Egypt): city of Amun, capital in the Middle and New Kingdoms; Karnak, Luxor, Valley of the Kings.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Abu Mena, south of Alexandria: early Christian pilgrimage centre, 5th-7th c. AD.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Nubian Monuments from Abu Simbel to Philae (Egypt), ten components.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Alexandria (Egypt): founded by Alexander the Great in 331 BC; Ptolemaic capital; Pharos lighthouse and Mouseion/Library.
sites.label: evidence (search-summary level)

sites.text: Tarraco (Tarragona): first and oldest Roman settlement on the Iberian Peninsula; capital of Hispania Citerior.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Augusta Emerita (Mérida), founded 25 BC by Augustus; capital of Lusitania.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Roman Walls of Lugo, 3rd-4th c. AD.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Emporion (Empúries, Catalonia): Phocaean Greek trading colony founded in the 6th c. BC (c. 575 BC), Palaiapolis then Neapolis; later Roman Emporiae.
sites.label: evidence (search-summary level)

sites.text: Massalia (Marseille): founded c. 600 BC by Greeks from Phocaea; foundation myth of Protis and Gyptis; archaeology supports early settlement on the Panier above the Lacydon.
sites.label: evidence (search-summary level; Pausanias 10.8.6 read)

sites.text: Naples: founded as Parthenope/Palaepolis, re-established as Neapolis in 470 BC.
sites.label: evidence

sites.text: Gadeira/Cadiz: Pausanias 10.4.6 records a custom of leaving the island at the command of Heracles.
sites.label: evidence

people.text: Homer: poet of the Iliad and Odyssey; Mycenaean culture inspired his epics (UNESCO).
people.label: evidence

people.text: Hesiod: poet of the Theogony and Works and Days; Muses of Helicon.
people.label: evidence

people.text: Pausanias: 2nd-c. AD travel writer; dates his Book 5 to 174 AD (Jones note).
people.label: evidence

people.text: Pheidias: sculptor of the gold-and-ivory Zeus at Olympia and the Athena of the Parthenon.
people.label: evidence

people.text: Alexander the Great (r. 336-323 BC): conquests to the Indus; death marks the Hellenistic period.
people.label: evidence

people.text: Philip II of Macedon (r. 360/359-336 BC); refounded Philippi 356 BCE.
people.label: evidence

people.text: Pericles: 'Age of Pericles' at Athens ca. 440-429 BC.
people.label: evidence

people.text: Callimachus: called Delos 'the most sacred of all islands'.
people.label: evidence

people.text: Libon of Elis: architect of the temple of Zeus at Olympia.
people.label: evidence

people.text: Battus: founder of Cyrene from Thera (Pausanias 10.15.6-7).
people.label: evidence

timeline.text: 2800-1100 BCE - Minoan civilisation; palatial centres 1900-1100 BCE.
timeline.label: evidence

timeline.text: 13th c. BC - first Acropolis fortification wall.
timeline.label: evidence

timeline.text: 8th c. BC - Delphic sanctuary and oracle develop; overseas colonisation.
timeline.label: evidence

timeline.text: 7th c. BCE - Phoenician port at Leptis Magna.
timeline.label: evidence

timeline.text: 548 BC - stone temple at Delphi burnt (Pausanias 10.5.13, Jones note).
timeline.label: evidence

timeline.text: ca. 510-507 BC - democracy introduced at Athens.
timeline.label: evidence

timeline.text: 323 BC - death of Alexander; Hellenistic period begins.
timeline.label: evidence

timeline.text: 146 BC - Roman rule of mainland Greece; Corinth sacked by Mummius.
timeline.label: evidence

timeline.text: 31 BC - Battle of Actium ends the Hellenistic period.
timeline.label: evidence
